newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition agrees to tax reform amendments.
newsitem.headline: German coalition agrees to tax reform amendments.

text.p: Germany's embattled coalition government agreed on Thursday on reforms to plug holes in the budget in coming years without raising taxes, but the plan was not certain to pass both houses of parliament.

Leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FPD), said they had agreed on an amended programme to help to negate projected gaping budget deficits in 1998 and 1999.
The coalition has teetered on the brink of collapse because the liberal FDP adamantly refused to consider tax increases proposed by the Christian Democrats to fill gaps in the 1997 and 1998 budgets.

Kohl's government, eager to qualify for the European Union's single currency, is desperately trying to push the 1997 deficit to levels below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the threshold for entry into economic and monetary union (EMU).

"We have finally agreed to the tax reform and changes to it," Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters after meetings of the three parliamentary parties in the coalition. "And it won't lead to bigger deficits."
But Waigel said the coalition had not discussed ways to plug a gaping hole in his budget for the current year, the year that matters for qualification for EMU.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, the CDU parliamentary leaders, said the amendments, which bring some reforms forward from 1999 to next year, would not mean that Germans would pay higher taxes.
"It is quite clear there will be no tax increases in 1998 at the end of the day," Schaeuble told reporters after addressing a CDU business forum in Bonn.
The tax reform is a mix of eliminating tax write-offs and lowering tax rates. It aims to lower tax levels for companies and individuals while making it more difficult to avoid taxes.
The reforms were originally intended to reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks ($17.5 billion) in 1999, but it was not clear if the amended plan would hit that target.

Schaeuble said the government was trying to repackage its tax reforms in a way which could gain the assent of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who can block tax measures through their control of the upper house of parliament.
But he said agreement on the tax reform would be possible only if the SPD dropped its two-year block on the government's attempt to scrap a capital trading tax on businesses.
The amended tax reform plan will be included in a draft bill to be put to the Bundestag (lower house) on June 26. Schaeuble said he expected the measures to clear the Bundestag without any problems.
